newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-NOAH LAUNCHES FRANCE ON QUEST FOR THIRD DAVIS CUP TITLE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-NOAH LAUNCHES FRANCE ON QUEST FOR THIRD DAVIS CUP TITLE.

text.p: Yannick Noah sets out on his personal quest for a third Davis Cup title on Friday, helped on the first stage by an injury to Mark Philippoussis.
Philippoussis is Australia's top singles player but will be missing from the line-up against captain Noah's French side in Sydney this weekend because of tendinitis in his arm.

The injury, which kept Philippoussis out of last month's Australian Open, is a big blow for the Australians on their return to the world group after two years in the wilderness of regional qualifiers.
But Australia, 26 times champions, have the huge advantage of one of the world's most successful doubles pairs of all time -- Mark Woodforde and Todd Woodbridge.
Nicknamed "The Woodies", the reigning Wimbledon, U.S. Open and Olympic champions have won 42 titles together and come into the tie fresh from their second triumph at the Australian Open.

Noah, who also captained France to victory in 1991, must decide whether to stick with Guy Forget and Guillaume Raoux, winners of the doubles in last year's thrilling final against Sweden, for what could prove the most crucial match of this weekend's tie.

Cedric Pioline, Arnaud Boetsch and Lionel Roux complete the squad again, as they did in snowy Malmo, and all except Pioline acclimatised themselves to the sunshine by playing in the Australian Open last month -- though none made it beyond the third round.
Australia have called up Sandon Stolle to replace Philippoussis in the singles, alongside Patrick Rafter.
Last year's runners-up Sweden begin the post-Edberg age with a home tie against Switzerland, who are themselves entering a new era following the retirement of Jakob Hlasek.
With Stefan Edberg taking retirement last December, after the final against France, Thomas Enqvist, ranked 10th in the world, spearheads the Swedish attack in Lulea, near the Arctic circle.
Enqvist and his team mates Magnus Larsson, Mikael Tillstrom and Nicklas Kulti start as favourites to beat the visitors, led by Marc Rosset, on the slow surface.

The United States, who won the last of their 31 Davis Cup titles in 1995, have a potentially difficult start to 1997 in the prosperous city of Ribeirao Preto, Brazil, site of some angry scenes last September when Austria walked out of a world group qualifying tie.
Austrian number one Thomas Muster stormed out of the doubles, saying Brazilian fans had spat at him and he was given a police escort to the airport.
The tie -- and the place in this year's world group -- went to Brazil by default.
The Americans will be without Andre Agassi, who has a twisted ankle, and Todd Martin, who has tendinitis in one knee.
German veteran Boris Becker has decided to miss another possible humiliation by in-form Spaniard Carlos Moya, the man who knocked him out of the Australian Open on the first day.
Former champions Germany will go to the island of Mallorca without Becker and Michael Stich for a clay-court tie which Spain firmly believe they can win.
In the singles, Australian Open finalist Moya will be joined by Alberto Costa, himself a quarter-finalist in Melbourne, while Alex Corretja will team up with Carlos Costa for the doubles.
Germany's weakened team comprises Bernd Karbacher -- another of Moya's victims in Melbourne, Hendrik Dreekmann, David Prinosil and Marc Goellner, who is recovering from injury.

A broken finger will keep world number five Yevgeny Kafelnikov out of Russia's first-round tie against South Africa in Durban where the heat, humidity and slow courts are likely to favour a home side led by Wayne Ferreira.
Dutch captain Stanley Franker is worried about his team's chances against Romania in Bucharest, in the absence of Wimbledon champion Richard Krajicek who is recovering from knee surgery.

Romania are back in the world group for the first time in 12 years and their top player, Adrian Voinea is ranked only 45th, compared to 21st for the top Dutchman available, Jan Simerink. But Franker warned against complacency after the surprise first-round defeat by India last year.
"Everybody expects it to be a piece of cake but this is really going to be tougher than the tie against India," he said.
India this time meet last year's semifinalists the Czech Republic on indoor clay in Pribram, near Prague.
Italy, who also made the semifinals last year, have recalled veteran Omar Camporese after a three-year absence for their tie against Mexico on the clay of the Foro Italico in Rome.
